title: What the Call Costs: Passing, Returning, and the Copy You Did Not Write

questions.question: A function takes std::vector<double> samples by value and is given a vector of 1024 doubles. What does the callee see?
options: A new buffer: one was allocated and all 1024 elements copied into it
The caller's buffer, since vectors are reference types
The caller's buffer, unless the callee modifies it
A new buffer, but only in a debug build
questions.explanation: Measured by comparing the address of the data: by value arrives as a new buffer, by const reference and by span arrive as the same one. Nothing in the source says a copy happened.

questions.question: The same vector is passed by value through two functions. How many buffers are allocated?
options: Two: the cost is per call, not once
One: the copy is shared between the two calls
None, because the compiler elides copies of parameters
Two, but only without optimisation
questions.explanation: Measured at two, against zero for const reference. A chain of five reading functions allocates and copies five times, and each line looks innocent on its own.

questions.question: A function builds a std::vector of 1024 doubles in a local and returns it by value. What arrives at the caller?
options: The same buffer the local held: it was handed over, not rebuilt
A copy of the buffer, which is why out parameters exist
A copy at -O0, and the same buffer at -O2
An empty vector, because the local was destroyed
questions.explanation: The same address arrives, at -O0 as well as -O2. Whether the compiler elided the local or moved it, the buffer travelled out. The out parameter version computes the same thing and costs a declaration, a non const result and a half filled state on early return.

questions.question: Why prefer rc::span<const double> over const std::vector<double>& for a function that only reads samples?
options: Neither copies, but the span also accepts a std::array or a pointer and a length from a driver, with no vector built
The span is faster to pass, being smaller
The span allows the function to modify the data
There is no difference; it is a style preference
questions.explanation: Measured against a vector, a std::array and a plain C array: the span took all three and copied none. A const vector reference would have required constructing a vector from the last two, which is the copy the signature was supposed to avoid.

questions.question: At what string length do the characters stop living inside the std::string object itself?
options: It depends on the standard library: measured at 16 here, with sizeof(std::string) of 32, and it is not a language rule
Always at 32, which is sizeof(std::string)
Always at 16, on every implementation
Never: a string's characters are always on the heap
questions.explanation: Characters were inside the object up to length 15 and on the heap from 16. That threshold is an implementation choice, so the suite prints the table and does not assert the number. It is why pass strings by const reference is advice about long strings.

questions.question: Why is return std::move(local); worse than return local; when returning a container?
options: It is unnecessary and can prevent the compiler eliding the local altogether
It copies instead of moving
It leaves the local in an undefined state the caller can observe
It is identical; both are fine
questions.explanation: Returning a named local plainly is the form that lets the compiler leave out the local entirely. Wrapping it in std::move turns it into an expression the elision rules do not cover, so the move happens where nothing needed to.
